messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Rabbi
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared, Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons, Shouting: Shouting
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David is a 63-year-old rabbi who came to treatment after months of telling himself he should be able to handle this on his own. He had arrived in the United States as a child refugee after armed men forced their way into his family’s neighborhood, shouting orders in the street and striking people with whatever they carried. What remains most vivid to him is not a complete story but sharply preserved moments: the sight of weapons in men’s hands, the sound of voices suddenly raised, and the shock of being grabbed and pulled before he understood what was happening. Even now, he says his body reacts before his mind does, as if it still lives in that earlier world. In session he speaks quietly, but when he describes those moments he becomes visibly tense, as though the old danger is present again.

For years David built a life that looked steady from the outside. He became a rabbi, known for warmth and composure, and he now lives with a long-term partner who has grown increasingly aware of how narrow his sense of safety has become. The difficulties intensified over the last few years as the congregation became larger and more physically informal. During greetings after services, an unexpected hand on his shoulder can make him flinch hard enough to lose his train of thought. If a visitor enters wearing something at the belt that resembles a weapon, or if a disagreement in the social hall turns into shouting, he feels himself pulled out of the present. In those moments he immediately tries to push his attention somewhere else—onto the order of the prayer books, the agenda for a committee meeting, the coffee urn—anything to distract himself from the rush in his body. He also grows more distant afterward, withholding affection and emotional openness from his partner because closeness leaves him feeling too exposed.

These episodes do not feel random to David. Each time he startles, he takes it as evidence that something is wrong with him: his body, in his words, has become an enemy that refuses to understand when he is safe. He has come to believe he cannot rely on himself if danger appears, and he compares himself harshly to an imagined stronger person who would have stopped what happened long ago. The trigger and the meaning arrive almost together; the raised voice or sudden touch does not just frighten him, it confirms his conviction that he is fundamentally unsteady. Once he is thinking this way, the world seems easier to ignite. A hand reaching for a friendly embrace, a ceremonial object held too abruptly, even loud enthusiasm from congregants can register first as threat, because he is already braced for proof that he is not in control.

That belief has narrowed his daily life. David now scans rooms automatically and chooses his seat in every setting—sanctuary, restaurant, family gathering—according to where he feels most protected, usually near an exit or against a wall where no one can come up behind him. He notices where voices are rising before he can follow what is being said, and his concentration fractures whenever he is trying to monitor the room. At work this has become painful: during pastoral meetings he sometimes realizes he has missed the thread of what someone is telling him because he was tracking movement in the doorway or the possibility that someone might touch him unexpectedly. The more he watches for danger, the more quickly he spots reminders of it, and ordinary noise or motion can take on the force of the past.

His efforts to manage this have, in his own mind, become further proof of personal failure. Because he keeps distracting himself and restricting how emotionally close he allows himself to be, he tells himself he deserves to suffer for what happened and for the ways he has disappointed others since. When he withdraws from his partner after being startled, he later judges himself as weak and unreliable; when he spends a whole meeting focused on where the exits are, he concludes that someone else would have coped better. Those judgments feed back into his vigilance. Feeling that he cannot depend on himself, he becomes even more careful about where he sits and how much of the world he lets in, and in that tightened state he is even more sensitive to shouting, to anything weapon-like, to the shock of unprepared touch.

What finally brought David to seek help was a recent Sabbath morning when a teenage congregant came up from behind to hug him in thanks after a service. David jerked away so abruptly that the boy looked frightened. He spent the rest of the day distracted and ashamed, certain that his own reactions had made him unsafe to others as well as to himself. At home that night, when his partner tried to comfort him, he pulled back again. He says he is afraid that his world will continue shrinking until only a few places feel tolerable, and that he will become a man who can preach refuge to others while unable to find any himself. He is hoping, cautiously, to learn whether his body can stop living in the old emergency, and whether closeness can feel possible without danger.
